danish.title: Anden bog (1805) — Kapitel 11
paragraphs: Næste dag vågnede han sent. Da han genkaldte sine friske indtryk, var den første tanke, der meldte sig, at han i dag skulle præsenteres for kejser Franz; han huskede krigsministeren, den høflige østrigske adjudant, Bilibin og gårsdagens samtale. Han klædte sig i fuld gallauniform, som han ikke havde båret i lang tid, og gik ind i Bilibins arbejdsværelse — frisk, livlig og smuk med sin forbundne hånd. I arbejdsværelset befandt sig fire herrer fra det diplomatiske korps. Med fyrst Hippolyte Kuragin (sekretær ved ambassaden) var Bolkonskij allerede bekendt. Bilibin introducerede ham for de andre.

De herrer, der var forsamlet hos Bilibin, var unge, velhavende, muntre selskabsfolk, der her som i Wien udgjorde en særlig kreds, som Bilibin, deres anfører, kaldte les nôtres (vores folk). Denne kreds, der næsten udelukkende bestod af diplomater, havde tydeligvis sine egne interesser, der intet havde at gøre med krig eller politik, men drejede sig om det fine selskab, visse kvinder og tjenestens officielle side. Disse herrer modtog fyrst Andrej som en af deres egne, en ære, de ikke udstrakte til mange. Af høflighed og for at få en samtale i gang stillede de ham nogle spørgsmål om hæren og slaget, hvorefter snakken gled over i muntre vittigheder og sladder.
»Vores folk.«

»Men det bedste af det hele var,« sagde en og fortalte om en diplomatkollega ulykke, »at kansleren sagde ham rent ud, at hans udnævnelse til London var en forfremmelse, og at han skulle betragte den som sådan. Kan I forestille jer hans mine? ...«
»Men det værste, mine herrer — jeg røber Kuragin for jer — er, at den stakkels mand lider, og denne Don Juan, den slyngel, udnytter det!«
Fyrst Hippolyte sad henslængt i en lænestol med benene over armlænet. Han begyndte at le.
»Fortæl mig om det!« sagde han.
»Åh, din Don Juan! Din slange!« råbte adskillige stemmer.

»Du ved ikke, Bolkonskij,« sagde Bilibin henvendt til fyrst Andrej, »at alle den franske hærs grusomheder (jeg havde nær sagt den russiske hærs) er ingenting sammenlignet med, hvad den mand har bedrevet blandt kvinderne!«
»La femme est la compagne de l'homme (kvinden er mandens ledsagerinde),« erklærede fyrst Hippolyte og begyndte at betragte sine hævede ben gennem en lorgnet.
»Kvinden er mandens ledsagerinde.«

Bilibin og resten af »vores folk« brast i latter lige i hovedet på Hippolyte, og fyrst Andrej indså, at Hippolyte, som han — det måtte han indrømme — næsten havde været jaloux på sin kones vegne, var denne kreds' skydeskive.
»Åh, jeg må byde dig på en oplevelse,« hviskede Bilibin til Bolkonskij. »Kuragin er udsøgt, når han taler politik — du skulle se hans værdighed!«
Han satte sig ved siden af Hippolyte og rynkede panden for at indlede en samtale om politik. Fyrst Andrej og de andre samlede sig omkring de to.

»Berlin-kabinettet kan ikke udtrykke en alliancefølelse,« begyndte Hippolyte, idet han kiggede vigtigt omkring sig på de andre, »uden at udtrykke ... som i sin seneste note ... forstår I ... Desuden, medmindre Hans Majestæt kejseren fraviger vores alliances princip ...«

»Vent, jeg er ikke færdig ...« sagde han til fyrst Andrej og greb ham i armen. »Jeg mener, at interventionen vil være stærkere end ikke-interventionen. Og ...« Han holdt en pause. »Man kan ikke tilskrive modtagelsesmanglerne vedrørende vor depeche af 18. november. Sådan ender det.« Og han slap Bolkonskijs arm for at tilkendegive, at han nu var ganske færdig.
»Demosthenes, jeg kender dig på den sten, du gemmer i din gyldne mund!« sagde Bilibin, og hårtotten på hans hoved bevægede sig tilfreds.
Alle lo, og Hippolyte højest af alle. Han var tydeligvis ulykkelig og trak vejret besværet, men kunne ikke holde den vilde latter tilbage, der rystede hans ellers ubevægelige ansigtstræk.

»Nå, mine herrer,« sagde Bilibin, »Bolkonskij er min gæst i dette hus og i Brünn i det hele taget. Jeg vil underholde ham, så godt jeg kan, med alle livets fornøjelser her. Var vi i Wien, ville det være let, men her i dette elendige mähriske hul er det vanskeligere, og jeg beder jer alle om hjælp. Brünns attraktioner må vises ham. Du kan tage dig af teatret, jeg af selskabslivet, og du, Hippolyte, naturligvis kvinderne.«
»Vi må lade ham møde Amélie, hun er udsøgt!« sagde en af »vores« og kyssede sine fingerspidser.
»Vi må i det hele taget vende denne blodtørstige soldat mod mere humane interesser,« sagde Bilibin.
»Jeg kan næppe benytte mig af Deres gæstfrihed, mine herrer, det er allerede tid for mig at gå,« svarede fyrst Andrej med et blik på sit ur.
»Hvorhen?«
»Til kejseren.«
»Åh! Åh! Åh!«
»Nå, farvel, Bolkonskij! Farvel, fyrste! Kom tidligt tilbage til middag,« råbte adskillige stemmer. »Vi tager os af dig.«
»Når du taler med kejseren, så prøv så vidt muligt at rose forsyningsvejene og ruteindikationerne,« sagde Bilibin og fulgte ham ud i forhallen.
»Jeg ville gerne tale godt om dem, men så vidt jeg kender kendsgerningerne, kan jeg ikke,« svarede Bolkonskij med et smil.
»Nå, tal bare så meget som muligt, under alle omstændigheder. Han har en passion for at give audiens, men han kan ikke lide at tale selv og kan det heller ikke, som du vil se.«

english.title: Book Two (1805) — Chapter 11
paragraphs: The next day he woke late. As his recent impressions came flooding back, the first thought in his mind was that today he had to be presented to Emperor Francis. He remembered the Minister of War, the courteous Austrian adjutant, Bilíbin, and last night's conversation. Having dressed in full parade uniform—which he hadn't worn in a long time—he went into Bilíbin's study looking fresh, lively, and handsome, with his hand still bandaged. Four gentlemen from the diplomatic corps were already in the study. Prince Andrew was already acquainted with Prince Hippolyte Kurágin, who served as a secretary to the embassy. Bilíbin introduced him to the others.

The gentlemen gathered at Bilíbin's were young, wealthy, fashionable men who formed a special circle both here and in Vienna. Bilíbin, their leader, called the group "ours." This set, made up almost entirely of diplomats, clearly had its own interests that had nothing to do with war or politics but revolved around high society, certain women, and the ceremonial side of government service. These gentlemen welcomed Prince Andrew as one of their own—an honor they extended to very few. Out of politeness, and to start a conversation, they asked him a few questions about the army and the battle, but then the talk quickly turned to lighthearted jokes and gossip.
"Ours."

"But the best part was," said one, telling the story of a fellow diplomat's misfortune, "that the Chancellor told him point-blank that his posting to London was a promotion and that he should treat it as such. Can you imagine the look on his face?"
"But the worst of it, gentlemen—and I'm giving Kurágin away here—is that the man is genuinely suffering, and this Don Juan, this scoundrel, is taking advantage of it!"
Prince Hippolyte was sprawled in a lounge chair with his legs thrown over the armrest. He started laughing.
"Tell me about that!" he said.
"Oh, you Don Juan! You snake!" cried several voices.

"You don't know this yet, Bolkónski," said Bilíbin, turning to Prince Andrew, "but all the horrors committed by the French army—I almost said the Russian army—are nothing compared to what this man has been doing to the women here!"
[Speaking in French] "Woman is man's companion," announced Prince Hippolyte, peering through a lorgnette at his own elevated legs.
"Woman is man's companion."

Bilíbin and the rest of "ours" burst out laughing right in Hippolyte's face, and Prince Andrew saw that Hippolyte—of whom, he had to admit, he had nearly been jealous on his wife's account—was the group's favorite target.
"Oh, I have to give you a treat," Bilíbin whispered to Bolkónski. "Kurágin is priceless when he talks politics—you have to see how serious he gets!"
He sat down next to Hippolyte, furrowed his brow, and began talking to him about politics. Prince Andrew and the others gathered around the two of them.

[Speaking in French] "The Berlin cabinet cannot express a sentiment of alliance," Hippolyte began, looking around importantly at the others, "without expressing... as in its last note... you understand... Besides, unless His Majesty the Emperor departs from the principle of our alliance..."

"Wait, I'm not finished..." he said to Prince Andrew, grabbing him by the arm. "I believe that intervention will prove stronger than non-intervention. And..." He paused. "Finally, one cannot attribute the non-receipt of our dispatch of November eighteenth. That is how it will end." And he released Bolkónski's arm to show he had quite finished.
"Demosthenes, I recognize you by the pebble hidden in your golden mouth!" said Bilíbin, and the tuft of hair on his head bobbed with satisfaction.
Everyone laughed, and Hippolyte louder than anyone. He was clearly embarrassed and breathing hard, but he couldn't contain the wild laughter that contorted his normally blank features.

"Well then, gentlemen," said Bilíbin, "Bolkónski is my guest here in this house and in Brünn itself. I want to show him the best time I can, with all the pleasures life here has to offer. If we were in Vienna it would be easy, but here in this miserable Moravian backwater it's harder, and I'm asking all of you to help me. You can handle the theater, I'll take care of society, and you, Hippolyte—the women, naturally."
"We absolutely must introduce him to Amelie—she's divine!" said one of "ours," kissing his fingertips.
"In general, we need to convert this bloodthirsty soldier to more civilized pursuits," said Bilíbin.
"I'm afraid I won't be able to take advantage of your hospitality, gentlemen. It's already time for me to go," replied Prince Andrew, glancing at his watch.
"Where to?"
"To see the Emperor."
"Oh! Oh! Oh!"
"Well, goodbye, Bolkónski! Goodbye, Prince! Come back early for dinner," called several voices. "We'll look after you."
"When you're speaking with the Emperor, try to say good things about the supply situation and the route planning," said Bilíbin, walking him to the hall.
"I'd like to speak well of them, but as far as I know the facts, I can't," replied Bolkónski with a smile.
"Well, talk as much as you can anyway. He has a passion for giving audiences, but he doesn't like talking himself and can't manage it, as you'll see."
